Where you’ll find them: They like to hang out in dark, concealed areas. “They hide in corners, underneath cabinets, in basements, sometimes in garages around the windows where flies may be active,” Potzler says. Size: Nickel-sized or less than a quarter of an inch (0.6 centimeters) long Color: Gray or brown, sometimes with white markings Can they harm you? Nope. 2 Wolf spider What they look like: There are over 200 species of wolf spiders crawling around, Potzler explains. And, since they’re hairy they can sometimes be mistaken for tarantulas. Also worth noting: “These are nomadic spiders that don’t spin webs to catch their prey—they hunt them down,” says Howard Russell, an entomologist at Michigan State University. Where you’ll find them: You can find wolf spiders where other insects reside—like garages, basements, sheds, and other dark, enclosed areas, according to Potzler. You can also find wolf spiders outside in various locations: In our around debris, underneath boards, or in gaps around your home. Size: Ranges up to 1 and 1/2 inches long Color: Gray, brown, or black Can they harm you? No: Russell assures that these spiders “would prefer to hide than bite.” Advertisement - Continue Reading Below 3 Black widow What they look like: The infamous black widow has a shiny black color along with their signature, red hourglass-shaped marking on their underside, explains Potzler. “They may also have red markings going up its back,” he adds. Where you’ll find them: Black widows prefer to dwell in places containing edges and corners, as well as tall grass, Russell notes. You can also find them hiding in mailboxes or garages, he adds. Size: 1/4 to 1/3 of an inch long Color: Black and red Can they harm you? “This is one of the few species of spider that can be dangerous to people,” says Potzler. “There are approximately 2,200 bites reported each year, but there has not been a death related to a widow spider in the U.S. since 1983.” Intense pain, muscle stiffness, possible nausea, and vomiting are the telltale signs of a black widow spider bite, and these symptoms will likely occur within a few hours after being bitten, Potzler explains. Head to the ER ASAP if you suspect you’ve been bitten to get immediate treatment. 4 Brown recluse What they look like: The brown recluse is a brown spider with a distinct “violin-shaped marking” on the top of its head and down its back, Potzler says. They also have six eyes instead of the eight that many other spiders have. Where you’ll find them: The brown recluse likes to hang out in undisturbed corners of homes, in sheds, and in basements or cellars. “Many bites occur because the spider is hiding in folded towels and sheets, underneath a pile of clothes on the floor, or in shoes in a closet,” Potzler says. “If you live in an area where brown recluse is common, it’s a good idea to shake out your clothes and shoes, or wear gloves if you are working in your shed or garage.” Size: Female bodies range from about 1⁄4 to 1⁄2 an inch with a leg span over 1 inch and males are generally half the size of females. Color: Brown Can they harm you? Yes. “The recluse can cause serious damage to people,” says Roberto M. Pereira, Ph.D., an insect research scientist with the University of Florida. “Bite sites are a serious problem.” A brown recluse bite can cause necrotizing wounds (meaning, it kills the cells and tissues around it), so you’ll want to see a doctor immediately if you think you’ve been bitten by one, Russell says. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below 5 Daddy longlegs What they look like: You’re probably pretty familiar with this one, but just in case: It has one round body part and very thin, long legs coming off of it. Where you’ll find them: They like to live outside, they can sometimes hide under siding or be found on and under decks. “For the most part, you’ll find them on the lawn or up in trees,” says Potzler. Size: Bodies range from the size of a pinhead to a quarter Color: Brown Can they harm you? No. “Contrary to myths found on the Internet, daddy longlegs are not venomous enough to kill a horse,” says Potzler. “They do not have venom glands. They pose no harm to humans.” 6 Hobo spider What they look like: Hobo spiders are tannish-brown and the top of the spider may look mottled, with darker and lighter spots, Potzler says. They look pretty hairy and have spiny hairs coming off the legs. Where you’ll find them: While they’re usually outside, they sometimes venture indoors. “It can hide in clothing, beds, and shoes,” Potzler says. Size: About 1/2 to 5/8 inches long Color: Light brown with pale markings Can they harm you? Yes. “The hobo spider can inflict a painful bite that results in localized red swelling and some pain, but no necrotic lesion,” Potzler says. Usually, symptoms will get better within 24 hours with OTC painkillers and ice. Abstract More than 40,000 species of spiders have been identified in the world. Spider bites is a common problem among people, however few of them are harmful but delay in treatment can cause death. Since the spider bites are risk full to human, they should be taken seriously, especially in endemic areas. Our objective in this review was to study about poisonous spiders and find out treatments of them. Therefore, we collected related articles from PubMed database and Google Scholar. Three important syndromes caused by spider bites are loxoscelism, latrodectism and funnel web spider syndrome. Many treatments are used but much more studies should have done to decrease the mortality. In this review, we describes different venomous spiders according to their appearance, symptoms after their bites and available treatments. Key Words: Spiders, spider bites, spider venoms, black widow spider, emergency treatment Introduction: Spiders belong to a branch of invertebrate animals called arthropods. Arthropods have the largest number of species. Along with ticks, mites and scorpions, spiders fall into the subphylum chelicerata and class of arachnids (1, 2). The arachnid class has very diverse members in a way that more than 80,000 species belonging to that class have been identified to date. Spiders are a large group of arachnids belonging to the araneae order (1). More than 40,000 species of spider have been identified to date but the real number is estimated at 4 times more than that number (3). Except for two small groups in the arachnid family, all spiders have poison glands and release their secretions into their venom sacs near their chelicerae. However, the majority of spiders do not bite humans and except for a few cases, they are not harmful to the human being or other mammals (2).Spider bites are common but the majority of species create little clinical presentations (3). There is only one aggressive spider named funnel-web in Australia, which attacks the human being without provocation. The majority of venomous spiders are found in Latin America. These large spiders are quite aggressive and their venom is pharmacologically highly toxic. Their bite results in severe pain, neurotoxic effects, diaphoresis, severe allergic reaction and priapism (1). Other spiders normally exhibit aggressive behavior after being trapped, injured or provoked. The severity of reactions to spider venom depends on factors such as its amount, site of biting and its duration and age and health condition. Mortality due to spider bite is rare (2). Spider venom includes different peptides and substances affecting sodium, calcium and potassium channels in neurons and also glutamate and acetylcholine receptors (4).Spider bite victims develop symptoms such as pain and swelling in the site of biting, necrosis, pyrexia, pulmonary edema, respiratory distress, hypertension, kidney dysfunction and death. Treatment protocol in the case of critically ill patients includes supportive measures and antivenom injection. Respiratory support and monitoring the hemodynamic status of these patients are of fundamental importance (5). Highly venomous spiders, funnel-web in Australia and armadeiras (armed spiders) in South America require antivenom and intensive therapeutic interventions (6). Three important syndromes are caused by spider bites: latrodectism, loxoscelism, and funnel-web spider syndrome (7). Here, we discuss about poisonous spiders and find out treatments of them. Introduction of venomous spiders This section describes different venomous spiders according to their appearance, symptoms after their bites and available treatments. Therefore, we collected related articles from PubMed and Google scholar (Figure 1). a) The brown recluse spider The brown recluse spider is recognized by the violin-shaped marking on its back (Figure 2). This spider takes rest during the day and is not aggressive but it will attack in the case of provocation. Patients are usually bitten by wearing clothes and shoes with spiders in them (2). Loxoscelism syndrome is the symptoms caused by the bite of the brown recluse spider. This spider's bite is usually painless but it later becomes an inflammatory, hemorrhagic and painful lesion (8). Necrosis spreads a few days following the bite and loxoscelism syndrome results in dermatitis necrosis in the site of biting, around which becomes red, white and blue, respectively (9). The venom of this spider contains hyaluronidase and sphingomyelinase D enzymes and results in necrosis. Moreover, neutrophil activity and platelet aggregation and thrombosis exacerbate necrosis (8). Local manifestations of the bite of this spider include edema, inflammation, hemorrhage, damage to the vessel wall, thrombosis, and necrosis (10) but systematic symptoms including acute renal failure, rhabdomyolysis and intravascular hemolysis have also been reported (11). In some cases, severe coagulopathy can result in stroke (7).Considering extensive differential diagnosis for skin necrosis, the standard criteria for the diagnosis of loxoscelism syndrome is capturing the spider during biting or capturing it in the place where biting occurred and its confirmation by a reliable arachnologist(12). ## Mini-report: likely spider species and why some bites matter

### Which spiders are most commonly mistaken for dangerous spiders in patients’ descriptions?

Patients often mistake common house spiders for dangerous species because the descriptions are similar or because the spiders are rarely seen. In the evidence, several common house spiders are highlighted as species that are easily confused with more feared spiders:

- **Common house spider** (Parasteatoda tepidariorum or Tegenaria domestica) is described as a “very common house spider” that can be mistaken for the **hobo spider** [N1-F1].  
- **Common house spider** and **spiders in the genus Steatoda** are sometimes mistaken for **black widow spiders** [N1-R3].  
- **Cellar spiders** are often mistaken for **brown recluses** because they are brownish, but they have much longer and thinner legs [N1-R5].  
- **Wolf spiders** are sometimes mistaken for **tarantulas** because they are hairy and nomadic [N1-F1].  

These patterns show that patients tend to overreact when a spider looks unfamiliar or when they associate a spider with a feared species, especially black widow or brown recluse.

### Which spiders are actually known to cause medically significant bites?

The evidence identifies a small group of spiders that are medically important and can cause clinically significant bites:

1. **Black widow**  
   - Known to be dangerous to people, with intense pain, muscle stiffness, nausea, and vomiting occurring within a few hours after a bite [N1-F1].  
   - The U.S. report notes that black widow bites are “one of the few species of spider that can be dangerous to people” and that victims should head to the ER ASAP [N1-F1].  
   - NIH/PMC evidence also groups black widow bites under **latrodectism**, one of the three important syndromes caused by spider bites [N2-R1].  

2. **Brown recluse**  
   - Associated with **loxoscelism**, a syndrome that can cause painless bites that later become inflammatory, hemorrhagic, and painful lesions, with necrosis spreading over days [N2-F2].  
   - The evidence notes that brown recluse bites can cause “serious damage to people” and that the wound can be necrotizing [N1-F1].  
   - Mayo Clinic and NIH/PMC evidence also note that brown recluse bites may take longer to heal and may leave a scar [N4-R1][N2-F2].  

3. **Hobo spider**  
   - Can inflict a painful bite that results in localized red swelling and some pain, but the evidence says no necrotic lesion [N1-F1].  
   - It is still considered “harmful” because the bite can be painful and should be treated with OTC painkillers and ice [N1-F1].  

4. **Funnel-web spider**  
   - The evidence explicitly states that funnel-web in Australia is the only aggressive spider named in the text that attacks humans without provocation [N2-F2].  
   - It is associated with **funnel web spider syndrome**, one of the three important syndromes [N2-R1].  

Other spiders described in the evidence are generally not considered medically important:
- **American house spider** and **daddy longlegs** are explicitly stated as “no harm” to humans [N1-F1].  
- **Wolf spider** is described as “would prefer to hide than bite” [N1-F1].  
- **Daddy longlegs** are not venomous enough to kill a horse and do not have venom glands [N1-F1].  

### How to distinguish harmless bites from bites that may need medical attention?

The evidence suggests a clear distinction between harmless and potentially harmful bites:

- **Harmless bites** usually heal on their own in a few days and do not need medical attention [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
- **Bites that may need medical attention** are those that:
  - Develop severe pain, worsening pain, or spreading pain and swelling [N5-R5].  
  - Include symptoms like fever, chills, or body aches, which may suggest infection [N5-R3].  
  - Involve difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling, which may indicate a severe allergic reaction [N5-R2].  
  - Include signs of a serious bite, such as an open sore, drainage, or severe swelling [N5-R5].  

The NIH/PMC evidence adds that the severity of reactions depends on factors such as venom amount, site of biting, duration, and the patient’s age and health condition [N3-R4]. It also notes that mortality due to spider bites is rare but delay in treatment can be dangerous [N2-F2].  

In short, patients should not assume every spider bite is dangerous. Most bites are harmless, but a few can cause significant symptoms. The key is to watch for worsening pain, spreading swelling, fever, difficulty breathing, or signs of infection or allergic reaction [N3-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. If those occur, medical care is needed [N3-R1][N5-R2].

## Mini-report: how patients should assess their own bite and next steps

### Symptoms that suggest a non-spider bite or a more serious reaction

The evidence gives several clues that may help patients decide whether the bite is likely to be non-spider-related or more serious:

1. **Non-spider bite symptoms**  
   - The evidence states that most spider bites usually heal on their own in about a week, and most non-venomous bites will improve within a couple of days and do not need medical attention [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
   - The most common symptoms described are small itchy bumps, irritated skin around the bite, and clearing up in a few days [N6-R3].  
   - If the bite does not match these typical patterns, it may be more concerning.

2. **More serious reaction symptoms**  
   - **Worsening pain or swelling** that spreads may indicate infection or a venomous bite [N5-R5].  
   - **Fever, chills, or body aches** may signal infection from a spider bite [N5-R3].  
   - **Difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling** can be signs of a severe allergic reaction [N5-R2].  
   - **Severe pain or swelling** that worsens or spreads may indicate an infection or a venomous bite [N5-R5].  
   - **Signs of necrosis** such as an open sore, drainage, or severe swelling may indicate a more serious bite [N5-R5].  

The NIH/PMC evidence also notes that spider bite victims can develop symptoms such as pain, swelling, necrosis, pyrexia, pulmonary edema, respiratory distress, hypertension, and even death, though mortality is rare [N4-R3][N2-F2]. That means patients should be especially alert for respiratory distress or severe systemic symptoms.

### When to seek urgent care versus when self-care is sufficient

The evidence provides a clear hierarchy for when to act:

- **Self-care is usually sufficient** if the bite is minor and typical of a common house spider or a harmless spider, and if symptoms are mild and resolving [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
- **Seek medical care immediately** if you suspect the bite is from a **black widow** or **brown recluse**, because these bites are known to be more serious [N5-R5][N1-F1].  
- **Seek urgent care** if there are symptoms of infection, allergic reaction, or severe local reaction:
  - Severe pain or swelling that worsens or spreads [N5-R5].  
  - Difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling [N5-R2].  
  - Fever, chills, or body aches [N5-R3].  
  - Open sore, drainage, or necrosis [N5-R5].  

The evidence also says to call the doctor’s office right away or go to the ER if fever, chills, or body aches appear after a spider bite [N5-R3]. That is a strong signal that medical evaluation is needed.

### What information patients should collect before seeing a doctor

To help a doctor make the best diagnosis, patients should collect the following information:

- **What they saw**  
  - The exact spider, if possible. The evidence notes that capturing the spider during biting or identifying it in the bite site is important for diagnosis [N2-F2].  
  - If the spider was not seen, describe the appearance, including body color, markings, leg shape, and whether it was hairy, long-legged, or had any distinctive features [N1-F1][N1-R5].  

- **When the bite happened**  
  - The timing is important because symptoms may develop quickly after a black widow bite or slowly after a brown recluse bite [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

- **Where the bite occurred**  
  - The evidence emphasizes that geography changes which spiders are likely suspects [N9]. Patients should note whether the bite happened at home, outdoors, in a shed, garage, basement, or other location [N1-F1][N1-R4].  

- **What symptoms are present**  
  - Pain, swelling, redness, itching, fever, chills, body aches, difficulty breathing, or changes in the wound [N5-R3][N5-R5].  

- **Any prior treatments**  
  - Whether they washed the area, applied cold packs, took painkillers, or did anything else [N4-R4].  

The evidence also notes that patients should bring the spider if possible, because capturing it during biting or identifying it in the bite site is part of the standard criteria for diagnosis [N2-F2]. This is especially important for brown recluse bites, which can be confused with other species [N1-R3][N1-R4].

### Bottom line for patients
If the bite is minor and typical, self-care and observation may be enough. But if symptoms worsen, spread, or involve fever, breathing difficulty, or signs of infection, patients should seek urgent care. Before seeing a doctor, they should note the spider’s appearance, when and where the bite happened, and what symptoms they have [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R3][N5-R5].

### How geography can change which spiders are likely suspects

Geography matters because the spiders that are common in one area may be rare or absent in another, and patients may mistake one species for another based on appearance.

- In the U.S. evidence, **common house spider** and **hobo spider** are confused because they are both common and similar-looking [N1-F1][N1-R4].

- **Cellar spiders** are mistaken for **brown recluses** because they are brownish and have long legs [N1-R5].  
- **Wolf spiders** are mistaken for **tarantulas** because they are hairy and nomadic [N1-F1].

### How local medical guidelines may differ for spider bites

The evidence suggests that local medical guidelines may differ because some spiders are more common in certain regions and some bites require more urgent evaluation.

- **Black widow** and **brown recluse** are explicitly noted as venomous spiders that can be dangerous to outdoor workers and are associated with serious syndromes [N2-R4][N2-F2].  
- The **Mayo Clinic** source says most spider bites heal on their own in about a week, while a recluse spider bite takes longer and may leave a scar [N4-R1].  
- **HealthLine** and **Harvard Health** both advise seeking immediate care for black widow or brown recluse bites or for signs of severe allergic reaction, difficulty breathing, or severe swelling [N5-R2][N5-R5].  
- The **PMC review** says that spider bites are common, but the majority of species create little clinical presentation and that mortality is rare, though delay in treatment can be dangerous [N2-F2].

That implies that in regions where funnel-web spiders are present, medical guidelines would emphasize urgent evaluation for a more aggressive bite than in areas where they are not common.

### Bottom line on regional clues
Patients should consider where they live because common spiders vary by region, and some species are easily mistaken for others. If a bite occurs in a house, basement, shed, or outdoor area, the likely suspects may include common house spiders, wolf spiders, cellar spiders, or hobo spiders, depending on location. Local medical guidelines may differ because some spiders are more common or more dangerous in specific areas, and because symptoms can vary by species and geography [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-R4][N2-F2]. Patients should note the spider’s appearance, the location of the bite, and any symptoms when seeking medical care.

# What kind of spider might have bitten you?

## Bottom line

Most spider bites are harmless, and many bites are from common house spiders that do not cause serious problems. However, a few spiders are medically important and can cause significant symptoms, so it’s important to pay attention to what happened, where it happened, and how you feel afterward.

If you’re asking, “what kind of spider might have bitten me?” the short answer is: **probably not a dangerous spider, but there are a few species that are more likely to matter**. The evidence supports this by showing that patients often mistake common house spiders for dangerous ones, and that only a small number of spider species are known to cause clinically significant bites [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## Which spiders are most likely to be mistaken for dangerous spiders?

The evidence shows that patients often confuse common spiders with feared species because the spiders look similar or are rarely seen.

- **Common house spider** is one of the most commonly encountered spiders and is often mistaken for the **hobo spider** [N1-R4].  
- **Common house spider** and **Steatoda** spiders are sometimes mistaken for the **black widow** [N1-R3].  
- **Cellar spiders** are often mistaken for **brown recluses** because they are brownish, but they have much longer and thinner legs [N1-R5].  
- **Wolf spiders** are sometimes mistaken for **tarantulas** because they are hairy and nomadic [N1-F1].  

In other words, if you describe a spider bite and say “I think it was a black widow or brown recluse,” it’s possible that the spider you actually saw was not one of those species, but a common house spider, cellar spider, hobo spider, or wolf spider [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5].

---

## Which spiders are actually known to cause medically significant bites?

The evidence identifies a small group of spiders that are medically important and can cause clinically significant bites:

### 1. Black widow
- **Why it matters**: Black widow bites are described as dangerous to people, with intense pain, muscle stiffness, nausea, and vomiting occurring within a few hours after a bite [N1-F1].  
- **Symptoms**: Pain, muscle stiffness, nausea, vomiting, and possible difficulty breathing [N1-F1][N2-R1].  
- **Medical advice**: If you suspect a black widow bite, you should head to the ER ASAP [N1-F1].  

### 2. Brown recluse
- **Why it matters**: Brown recluse bites are associated with **loxoscelism**, a syndrome that can cause painless bites that later become inflammatory, hemorrhagic, and painful lesions, with necrosis spreading over days [N2-F2].  
- **Symptoms**: Pain, swelling, necrosis, and sometimes fever, respiratory distress, or severe systemic effects [N2-F2][N4-R3].  
- **Medical advice**: If you suspect a brown recluse bite, you should seek medical care immediately [N1-F1].  

### 3. Hobo spider
- **Why it matters**: Hobo spider bites can cause a painful bite with localized red swelling and some pain, but they do not cause necrotic lesions [N1-F1].  
- **Medical advice**: These bites are still “harmful,” and OTC painkillers and ice are recommended, but they are not as severe as black widow or brown recluse bites [N1-F1].  

### 4. Funnel-web spider
- **Why it matters**: The evidence explicitly says funnel-web in Australia is the only aggressive spider named in the text that attacks humans without provocation [N2-F2].  
- **Why it matters medically**: It is associated with **funnel web spider syndrome**, one of the three important syndromes caused by spider bites [N2-R1].  

Other spiders described in the evidence are generally not considered medically important:
- **American house spider** and **daddy longlegs** are explicitly stated as “no harm” to humans [N1-F1].  
- **Wolf spider** is described as “would prefer to hide than bite” [N1-F1].  
- **Daddy longlegs** are not venomous enough to kill a horse and do not have venom glands [N1-F1].  

So, if you are asking, “what kind of spider might have bitten me?” the safest interpretation is: **it was probably a common spider, not one of the few that are medically dangerous** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## How to tell whether your bite is harmless or may need medical attention

The evidence gives a clear way to decide whether a bite is likely harmless or whether medical care is needed.

### Harmless bites usually:
- Heal on their own in a few days or a week [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
- Cause small itchy bumps, irritated skin around the bite, and clearing up quickly [N6-R3].  
- Do not cause severe pain, spreading swelling, fever, or difficulty breathing [N3-R1][N5-R5].  

### Bites that may need medical attention include:
- Worsening pain or swelling that spreads [N5-R5].  
- Fever, chills, or body aches [N5-R3].  
- Difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling [N5-R2].  
- Signs of infection, such as open sore, drainage, or severe swelling [N5-R5].  
- Symptoms that match a serious syndrome, such as necrosis, respiratory distress, or severe systemic effects [N2-F2].  

The NIH/PMC review also notes that the severity of reactions depends on factors such as venom amount, site of biting, duration, and the patient’s age and health condition [N3-R4]. It also says that mortality due to spider bites is rare, but delay in treatment can be dangerous [N2-F2].  

So, if you have only a small, itchy bite that is improving, self-care is probably enough. But if the bite worsens, spreads, or you develop fever, difficulty breathing, or severe pain, you should seek care [N3-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5].

---

## What you should do next

### 1. Collect information before seeing a doctor
If you want the best answer, bring the following details:
- **What you saw**: If you saw the spider, describe its appearance, including body color, markings, leg shape, and whether it was hairy, long-legged, or had any distinctive features [N1-F1][N1-R5].  
- **When the bite happened**: The timing matters because symptoms can develop quickly after a black widow bite or slowly after a brown recluse bite [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Where the bite occurred**: Note whether it happened at home, outdoors, in a shed, garage, basement, or other location [N1-F1][N1-R4].  
- **What symptoms you have**: Pain, swelling, redness, itching, fever, chills, body aches, difficulty breathing, or changes in the wound [N5-R3][N5-R5].  
- **Any prior treatments**: Whether you washed the area, applied cold packs, took painkillers, or did anything else [N4-R4].  

### 2. Know what to watch for
If you suspect a dangerous spider bite, the evidence says:
- **Seek immediate medical care** if you think you were bitten by a **black widow** or **brown recluse** [N5-R5][N1-F1].  
- **Seek urgent care** if you have severe pain, spreading swelling, fever, difficulty breathing, or signs of infection or allergic reaction [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5].  

### 3. What to do if you can’t bring the spider
The evidence says that capturing the spider during biting or identifying it in the bite site is important for diagnosis [N2-F2]. If you can’t bring the spider, describe it carefully so the doctor can compare it with known species [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## Regional clues and why location matters

The evidence shows that geography can change which spiders are likely suspects. In the U.S. evidence, **common house spiders, hobo spiders, cellar spiders, and wolf spiders** are all common and can be confused with more feared species [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-R5].  

### What that means for you
- If you live in an area where hobo spiders are common, you may mistake them for black widows or brown recluses [N1-R4].  
- If you live in an area where cellar spiders are common, you may mistake them for brown recluses [N1-R5].  
- If you live in an area where wolf spiders are common, you may mistake them for tarantulas [N1-F1].  

### How local guidelines may differ
Local medical guidelines may differ because some spiders are more common in certain regions and some bites require more urgent evaluation. The evidence notes that **black widow** and **brown recluse** are venomous spiders that can be dangerous to outdoor workers [N2-R4], and that brown recluse bites may take longer to heal and may leave a scar [N4-R1].  

So, even if you are not in an area where funnel-web spiders are present, your local guidelines may still emphasize evaluation for black widow or brown recluse bites if the symptoms are concerning [N2-R4][N2-F2].

---

## Final advice

If you are asking, “what kind of spider might have bitten me?” the answer is:

- **Most likely not a dangerous spider.**  
- **Common house spiders, cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders** are the most commonly encountered and are often mistaken for dangerous spiders [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5].  
- **Black widow and brown recluse** are the only spiders in the evidence that are clearly medically important and can cause serious bites [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **If the bite is minor and improving, self-care is probably enough.**  
- **If the bite worsens, spreads, or you develop fever, difficulty breathing, or severe pain, you should see a doctor right away** [N3-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5].  
- **If you can, bring the spider or describe it carefully** so the doctor can help you figure out what happened [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

In short: the evidence suggests you are more likely to have been bitten by a common, harmless spider than by a dangerous one, but it’s important to watch for symptoms and seek care if needed [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-R2].

## Mini-report: likely spider species and why some bites matter

### Which spiders are most commonly mistaken for dangerous spiders in patients’ descriptions?

Patients often mistake common house spiders for dangerous species because the descriptions are similar or because the spiders are rarely seen. In the evidence, several common house spiders are highlighted as species that are easily confused with more feared spiders:

- **Common house spider** (Parasteatoda tepidariorum or Tegenaria domestica) is described as a “very common house spider” that can be mistaken for the **hobo spider** [N1-F1].  
- **Common house spider** and **spiders in the genus Steatoda** are sometimes mistaken for **black widow spiders** [N1-R3].  
- **Cellar spiders** are often mistaken for **brown recluses** because they are brownish, but they have much longer and thinner legs [N1-R5].  
- **Wolf spiders** are sometimes mistaken for **tarantulas** because they are hairy and nomadic [N1-F1].  

These patterns show that patients tend to overreact when a spider looks unfamiliar or when they associate a spider with a feared species, especially black widow or brown recluse.

### Which spiders are actually known to cause medically significant bites?

The evidence identifies a small group of spiders that are medically important and can cause clinically significant bites:

1. **Black widow**  
   - Known to be dangerous to people, with intense pain, muscle stiffness, nausea, and vomiting occurring within a few hours after a bite [N1-F1].  
   - The U.S. report notes that black widow bites are “one of the few species of spider that can be dangerous to people” and that victims should head to the ER ASAP [N1-F1].  
   - NIH/PMC evidence also groups black widow bites under **latrodectism**, one of the three important syndromes caused by spider bites [N2-R1].  

2. **Brown recluse**  
   - Associated with **loxoscelism**, a syndrome that can cause painless bites that later become inflammatory, hemorrhagic, and painful lesions, with necrosis spreading over days [N2-F2].  
   - The evidence notes that brown recluse bites can cause “serious damage to people” and that the wound can be necrotizing [N1-F1].  
   - Mayo Clinic and NIH/PMC evidence also note that brown recluse bites may take longer to heal and may leave a scar [N4-R1][N2-F2].  

3. **Hobo spider**  
   - Can inflict a painful bite that results in localized red swelling and some pain, but the evidence says no necrotic lesion [N1-F1].  
   - It is still considered “harmful” because the bite can be painful and should be treated with OTC painkillers and ice [N1-F1].  

4. **Funnel-web spider**  
   - The evidence explicitly states that funnel-web in Australia is the only aggressive spider named in the text that attacks humans without provocation [N2-F2].  
   - It is associated with **funnel web spider syndrome**, one of the three important syndromes [N2-R1].  

Other spiders described in the evidence are generally not considered medically important:
- **American house spider** and **daddy longlegs** are explicitly stated as “no harm” to humans [N1-F1].  
- **Wolf spider** is described as “would prefer to hide than bite” [N1-F1].  
- **Daddy longlegs** are not venomous enough to kill a horse and do not have venom glands [N1-F1].  

### How to distinguish harmless bites from bites that may need medical attention?

The evidence suggests a clear distinction between harmless and potentially harmful bites:

- **Harmless bites** usually heal on their own in a few days and do not need medical attention [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
- **Bites that may need medical attention** are those that:
  - Develop severe pain, worsening pain, or spreading pain and swelling [N5-R5].  
  - Include symptoms like fever, chills, or body aches, which may suggest infection [N5-R3].  
  - Involve difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling, which may indicate a severe allergic reaction [N5-R2].  
  - Include signs of a serious bite, such as an open sore, drainage, or severe swelling [N5-R5].  

The NIH/PMC evidence adds that the severity of reactions depends on factors such as venom amount, site of biting, duration, and the patient’s age and health condition [N3-R4]. It also notes that mortality due to spider bites is rare but delay in treatment can be dangerous [N2-F2].  

In short, patients should not assume every spider bite is dangerous. Most bites are harmless, but a few can cause significant symptoms. The key is to watch for worsening pain, spreading swelling, fever, difficulty breathing, or signs of infection or allergic reaction [N3-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. If those occur, medical care is needed [N3-R1][N5-R2].

## Mini-report: how patients should assess their own bite and next steps

### Symptoms that suggest a non-spider bite or a more serious reaction

The evidence gives several clues that may help patients decide whether the bite is likely to be non-spider-related or more serious:

1. **Non-spider bite symptoms**  
   - The evidence states that most spider bites usually heal on their own in about a week, and most non-venomous bites will improve within a couple of days and do not need medical attention [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
   - The most common symptoms described are small itchy bumps, irritated skin around the bite, and clearing up in a few days [N6-R3].  
   - If the bite does not match these typical patterns, it may be more concerning.

2. **More serious reaction symptoms**  
   - **Worsening pain or swelling** that spreads may indicate infection or a venomous bite [N5-R5].  
   - **Fever, chills, or body aches** may signal infection from a spider bite [N5-R3].  
   - **Difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling** can be signs of a severe allergic reaction [N5-R2].  
   - **Severe pain or swelling** that worsens or spreads may indicate an infection or a venomous bite [N5-R5].  
   - **Signs of necrosis** such as an open sore, drainage, or severe swelling may indicate a more serious bite [N5-R5].  

The NIH/PMC evidence also notes that spider bite victims can develop symptoms such as pain, swelling, necrosis, pyrexia, pulmonary edema, respiratory distress, hypertension, and even death, though mortality is rare [N4-R3][N2-F2]. That means patients should be especially alert for respiratory distress or severe systemic symptoms.

### When to seek urgent care versus when self-care is sufficient

The evidence provides a clear hierarchy for when to act:

- **Self-care is usually sufficient** if the bite is minor and typical of a common house spider or a harmless spider, and if symptoms are mild and resolving [N3-R1][N4-R1].  
- **Seek medical care immediately** if you suspect the bite is from a **black widow** or **brown recluse**, because these bites are known to be more serious [N5-R5][N1-F1].  
- **Seek urgent care** if there are symptoms of infection, allergic reaction, or severe local reaction:
  - Severe pain or swelling that worsens or spreads [N5-R5].  
  - Difficulty breathing, elevated heart rate, or facial swelling [N5-R2].  
  - Fever, chills, or body aches [N5-R3].  
  - Open sore, drainage, or necrosis [N5-R5].  

The evidence also says to call the doctor’s office right away or go to the ER if fever, chills, or body aches appear after a spider bite [N5-R3]. That is a strong signal that medical evaluation is needed.

### What information patients should collect before seeing a doctor

To help a doctor make the best diagnosis, patients should collect the following information:

- **What they saw**  
  - The exact spider, if possible. The evidence notes that capturing the spider during biting or identifying it in the bite site is important for diagnosis [N2-F2].  
  - If the spider was not seen, describe the appearance, including body color, markings, leg shape, and whether it was hairy, long-legged, or had any distinctive features [N1-F1][N1-R5].  

- **When the bite happened**  
  - The timing is important because symptoms may develop quickly after a black widow bite or slowly after a brown recluse bite [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

- **Where the bite occurred**  
  - The evidence emphasizes that geography changes which spiders are likely suspects [N9]. Patients should note whether the bite happened at home, outdoors, in a shed, garage, basement, or other location [N1-F1][N1-R4].  

- **What symptoms are present**  
  - Pain, swelling, redness, itching, fever, chills, body aches, difficulty breathing, or changes in the wound [N5-R3][N5-R5].  

- **Any prior treatments**  
  - Whether they washed the area, applied cold packs, took painkillers, or did anything else [N4-R4].  

The evidence also notes that patients should bring the spider if possible, because capturing it during biting or identifying it in the bite site is part of the standard criteria for diagnosis [N2-F2]. This is especially important for brown recluse bites, which can be confused with other species [N1-R3][N1-R4].

### Bottom line for patients
If the bite is minor and typical, self-care and observation may be enough. But if symptoms worsen, spread, or involve fever, breathing difficulty, or signs of infection, patients should seek urgent care. Before seeing a doctor, they should note the spider’s appearance, when and where the bite happened, and what symptoms they have [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R3][N5-R5].
